n: David calls the Lord his rock and begs him not to stay silent. If God doesn’t answer, David feels he will be like the dead.

f.g: The grave or the realm of the dead (Sheol).

n: Raising hands was the ancient posture of prayer. David stretches his hands toward the innermost room of the sanctuary where God’s presence dwelt.

f.g: The Most Holy Place (Holy of Holies), the inner sanctuary where the ark rested.

n: He asks not to be dragged off with hypocrites who speak friendly words while plotting harm. Their smooth talk hides cruel hearts.

f.w: speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief is in their hearts

n: David asks that the wicked receive what their deeds deserve. This is a plea for justice, leaving vengeance in God’s hands rather than his own.
Because they ignore what God is doing in the world, they will be torn down rather than built up. Blindness to God leads to ruin.

f.g: A building image: God tears down and builds up nations and people.

n: The turning point: David blesses the Lord because his prayer has been heard. The psalm moves from plea to praise.
God is both strength and shield — power to act and protection from harm. Trusting him brings help, and help brings a song.
God strengthens all his people and especially his anointed king. “Anointed” in Hebrew is mashiaḥ — Messiah — pointing beyond David to Christ.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ; Greek christos — the root of the titles Messiah and Christ.

n: David ends praying for the whole nation: save them, bless them, and shepherd them forever. “Feed them” pictures God as a shepherd carrying his flock.

f.g: Shepherd them, tend them as a flock.
